newsitem.title: UK: World leaders see continuity in Clinton victory.
newsitem.headline: World leaders see continuity in Clinton victory.

text.p: World leaders on Wednesday hailed Bill Clinton's re-election as U.S. president, seeing it as signifying continuity in the crucial American role in international affairs.
In early reaction to Clinton's resounding victory over Republican Bob Dole, Arab countries expressed hopes he would now be able to push forward the faltering Middle East peace process.
Israel confined itself to giving Clinton its "blessing" and an assumption that traditionally strong relations between the two countries would continue.

In Asia, China saw Clinton's win enhancing prospects for better bilateral ties while Japan, which has just held its own general election, looked forward to "world peace and prosperity" with Clinton still in the White House.

In Europe, French President Jacques Chirac and British Prime Minister John Major were among the first to congratulate Clinton while European Union officials hailed the result as a guarantee of continued cooperation from an experienced president with a fully trained team.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, recovering after heart surgery, is to send a message of congratulation to Clinton, Kremlin sources said.
Yeltsin was informed of the election result in his hospital bed. The two leaders enjoy cordial relations.
Russian foreign policy experts say the Kremlin will have been relieved at Clinton's victory as it prefers continuity and has less confidence in the Republicans.

President Nelson Mandela of South Africa was the first African leader to congratulate Clinton, expressing the hope that his country's relations with the United States would continue to improve through Clinton's second term of office.
Middle East reaction came thick and fast, with the Palestinians leading calls for an increased U.S. role in promoting peace in the region.
"We consider the victory of President Clinton a positive step towards a comprehensive, just and permanent peace in the Middle East," Palestinian Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei told Reuters.
"It is high time that the U.S. plays an active role in the peace talks between Palestinians and Israelis and acts as a referee," Korei said.
His words were echoed in Jordan and Egypt.

"We welcome Mr Clinton's re-election," Jordanian Information Minister Marwan Muasher said. "We think he has been very instrumental in pushing the peace process forward and we hope he will do even more in terms of getting the peace process out of its present crisis.
"We think his re-election opens the door for a more active role by the U.S. and we would welcome this," he told Reuters.

Egyptian Information Minister Safwat el-Sherif, interviewed on the Arabic service of the BBC, commented: "I don't believe U.S. priorities will change. On the contrary, the election of President Bill Clinton shows the continuity of U.S. policies and U.S. priorities, especially towards international relations and the Middle East."

"The presence of President Clinton and his administration and his election...gives confidence that this partner will continue the peace process and will do everything possible to narrow the gap between points of views."

Israel's first reaction came from Foreign Minister David Levy, who told army radio: "(I convey) a blessing in the name of the government of Israel, and I can say in the name of all the citizens of Israel, to President Bill Clinton.
"I have no doubt that our relations will continue and strengthen in the future," Levy said.
Asian financial markets moved higher, apparently happy that the Democrat Clinton had retained the presidency but that the Republicans had kept control of Congress.
A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters: "We wish to congratulate President Clinton on his re-election.
"Now, a good opportunity has presented itself for improving and expanding Sino-U.S. relations," the Beijing spokesman said.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was unstinting in his praise for Clinton's victory, saying he congratulated the president "from the bottom of my heart".
"The people of the United States made a very great choice," Hashimoto told reporters.
"President Clinton's re-election reassures us of world peace and prosperity," Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said.
Vietnam, for years the bitter enemy of the United States, also welcomed the victory of Clinton, the man who normalised relations between Washington and Hanoi in 1995.

"On our side, Vietnam hopes the cooperative relationship between Vietnam and the United States will continue to develop for the benefit of the two countries and the benefit of peace, stability, cooperation and development in the region and world," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.

In Europe, French President Chirac was effusive in his congratulations, saying Clinton's re-election guaranteed France a "friendly, clear-sighted, competent and generous" U.S. partner towards the new millennium.
In a message addressed "Mr President, My dear Bill", Chirac praised Clinton's "wise statesmanship" and said his victory was "joyful news".
British Prime Minister Major said Clinton had received a resounding vote of confidence from the American people.

"The president has campaigned on his record and his economic and political achievements have spoken for themselves. The prime minister looks forward to continuing to work closely with the president over the next four years," an official statement said.
